dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the Next.js/Vite contract from vendored source

evidence.note: Extensive upfront orientation: reads test runner, next-shims.d.ts contract files, plugin-rsc types/options/runtime-entry types/README/examples, and catalogs every next/* import plus named imports per module across fixtures before writing code — grounding signatures in vendored types and fixtures.

During implementation, traces plugin-rsc dev middleware/serverHandler and full config hook, checks html-stream helpers and rsc-html-stream, and reads streaming test expectations — resolving mechanics from upstream source rather than memory.

Mines npm dist trees deeply: cats plugin-rsc plugin.d.ts/index.d.ts, greps renderToString in react-dom, and reads actual plugin-rsc compiled .js with targeted sed ranges to understand serverHandler/config resolution — tracing how plugin-rsc actually implements things.

Hypothesis-driven behavioral probing: reproduces an undici Request-construction error, tests multiple Request/init construction forms and NextRequest semantics empirically to resolve a specific ambiguity as it surfaced during debugging.

Cross-checks fixtures/test specs as an executable contract: reads metadata fixtures, app-router and nextjs-compat metadata specs, route handlers/actions, and config-redirect test before implementing those subsystems.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent performs both a thorough upfront contract-reverse-engineering pass (shims, plugin-rsc types/README/examples, import catalog) and sustained, hypothesis-driven investigation throughout the build — repeatedly returning to upstream plugin-rsc .js/.d.ts and react-dom source to resolve specific ambiguities (steps 67-105, 255-279), empirically probing undici Request behavior (399-415), and using fixtures/test specs as an executable spec (172-206). This exceeds the level-8 'systematic mining + cross-check' anchor and displays most level-10 markers (returning to source to resolve behavioral ambiguities, tracing implementation, tests-as-spec); I place it at 9 rather than 10 given limited visible depth of next-source TypeScript reading and some bulk-written shims.

dimensions.name: Structuring the build across subsystems and routers

evidence.note: Extended recon phase reading fixtures, contracts, and tests before decomposing — grounds the milestone breakdown in understanding rather than guessing.

Five explicit TaskCreate milestones defining distinct subsystems in dependency order: scaffolding/build → next/* shims (resolution) → app router+SSR → pages router+SSG → CLI+middleware. Foundational pieces sequenced before dependent features.
TaskUpdate status transitions (in_progress→completed→next) show the milestone plan was tracked and used through execution, not just authored once.

First full test run occurs only after nearly all subsystems are written; milestones completed by functional scope coverage rather than a concrete per-milestone done-signal (fixture render / test subset passing).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced an explicit, dependency-ordered milestone plan (steps 58-62) with foundational pieces (scaffolding, module-resolution shims, dev server) sequenced before dependent features (routers, SSG, actions), and tracked those milestones to completion via TaskUpdate — clearly exceeding the flat/unordered anchor-3 and the loose anchor-5. However, milestone done-criteria were scope-based ('implement these shims/routers') rather than tied to concrete verifiable signals like a fixture app rendering or a specific test subset passing, and tests were deferred to the end (step 344) rather than gating each milestone, so it falls short of the anchor-8 requirement for concrete per-milestone done-signals. This places it at a 6.

dimensions.name: Using and extending the test suite as a correctness oracle

evidence.note: The agent wrote the entire system (CLI, all shims, both routers, SSR, SSG, metadata, middleware, actions, client entries) across ~280 steps without running a single test or booting any app — subsystems declared done purely by inspection, the opposite of incremental verification.

The full run_tests.sh suite is executed only twice, both very late, used as a coarse pass/fail gauge; intervening steps 349-369 are mostly npm-install/env fixing rather than test-driven correctness work.
Late manual spot-check: boots the app-basic dev server, backgrounds it, probes with curl, and reads the 500 error body/log — genuine finer-grained verification beyond the full suite.

Tight isolation of one bug: focused micro-reproduction scripts for the undici Request-construction failure ('Reproduce undici error', 'Probe undici request-as-init', 'Test NextRequest semantics') before editing — real failure isolation, but backloaded and narrow to a single subsystem.
Reads test runner and specific spec files upfront to understand expectations, but this is contract-understanding rather than an active verification loop.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent exceeds anchor 3 because it does perform finer-grained verification and isolates failures — booting a fixture dev server, curl-probing, and building targeted undici reproduction scripts. But it falls short of anchor 5's 'runs run_tests.sh regularly and uses failures to guide fixes,' since the suite is run only twice and very late while the entire build proceeded by inspection with no verification loop. The tight per-subsystem loops of anchor 8 appear only in the final debugging phase for one bug, not as a sustained strategy, so the observed level lands at 4.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-count and remaining scope across a long build

evidence.note: Maintained a task list (TaskCreate/TaskUpdate, marking subsystems in_progress/completed), giving a structural sense of remaining scope, though not a pass/fail picture.
Counted total tests and read run_tests.py/spec files, showing awareness of overall test scope early on.
Wrote nearly the entire implementation before running the suite once — a long build stretch with no live pass-count feedback, indicating little continuous trajectory monitoring.
Full test-suite runs occur late and are followed by build/install environment troubleshooting rather than any visible pass-count delta or failure-to-subsystem mapping.
Ends in single-issue app-basic/undici debugging with no visible regression tracking or thrash detection; trajectory truncates before tests pass.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows scope awareness — a subsystem task list and an early test count — but builds almost everything before its first suite run, so there is no live pass/fail trajectory across the long build, matching the level-3 anchor ('occasionally notes scope but doesn't track regressions or map failures to subsystems') rather than level 5's running pass-count sense with regression detection. No observable evidence of pass-count deltas, baseline comparison, or thrash detection appears, though the digest's omission of prose/observations lowers my confidence.

dimensions.name: Revising approach as the contract and constraints emerge

evidence.note: Rewrote pages handler.ts after reading the instrumentation test, and corrected the handlePagesRequest signature/wiring across entry.rsc and handler via edits and a sed patch — revising a subsystem when the contract emerged rather than patching symptoms blindly.
Fully rewrote link.tsx after reading the link-test fixture (323 Read, 326 read fixture, 329 Write), adapting the shim to the discovered behavioral contract.

First full test run couldn't execute; agent investigated node_modules/offline npm, changed packaging strategy (added optional peers in package.json 368), reinstalled and re-ran — adapting the delivery approach to environment reality.

Strongest adaptation: dev server 500 -> isolated and reproduced the undici new Request() error, probed multiple Request-construction forms (399-415), re-examined the assumption, then propagated the fix to both server.tsx and entry.rsc and rebuilt/reinstalled. Deliberate root-cause re-examination, though not re-confirmed against the suite before the trajectory ends.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows clear, evidence-driven course corrections: re-orienting mid-build against the tests/reference (221-279), revising subsystems (handler, link) when fixtures contradicted assumptions, and a genuinely deliberate root-cause loop for the undici Request bug that it propagated across affected files (388-428). This is above the level-5 'backs out a wrong design after reasonable evidence' and approaches the level-8 'treats surprising failures as signals to re-examine assumptions.' It falls short of 8 because corrections are mostly local/wiring/packaging rather than architectural, the strong adaptation is concentrated late rather than sustained, and the final fixes are not confirmed against the test suite within the trajectory.

rubric.task_read: The agent must build 'vinext' — a from-scratch Vite-based reimplementation of a large Next.js feature surface (dual routers, SSR, SSG, server actions, middleware, caching, a next/* interception plugin, CLI, CJS support) into a single package, using only vendored reference source and no next dependency. This is an extremely long-horizon, high-complexity build with an under-specified contract that must be reverse-engineered from vendored source and fixture shim files, and a concrete 335→373-test acceptance oracle. It demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep reference-reading, layered decomposition across many subsystems, disciplined use of the test suite as a verification loop, and continual course-correction as the API contract is discovered.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the Next.js/Vite contract from vendored source
dimensions.description: Reading the vendored next/vite source, fixture next-shims.d.ts contracts, and test fixtures to infer exact API signatures and behavior before/while implementing each subsystem.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The contract is implicit: no docs, no internet, and correctness is defined by upstream behavior and the shim type signatures. Guessing signatures for useRouter, getStaticProps, after(), or the Vite plugin hooks leads to silent, compounding failure across dozens of tests.

anchors.0: Starts coding vinext from memory of Next.js APIs without opening the vendored source or shim files.
anchors.3: Skims one or two files (e.g. a shim) but largely relies on prior knowledge; misses how Vite plugin hooks or RSC actually resolve modules.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant next-shims.d.ts contracts and the key vite plugin API before implementing each major subsystem, grounding signatures in the vendored types.
anchors.8: Systematically mines both the npm dist trees and the next-source TypeScript for the mechanics of each subsystem (routing, SSR, caching, server actions), cross-checks against fixture apps and the test files to learn expected behavior, and records the discovered contract.
anchors.10: Sustains targeted, hypothesis-driven investigation across the whole build — repeatedly returning to upstream source to resolve specific behavioral ambiguities as they surface, tracing how vite@8/plugin-rsc implement resolution and hydration, and using fixtures/tests as an executable spec so nearly every implementation choice is evidence-backed rather than guessed.

dimensions.name: Structuring the build across subsystems and routers
dimensions.description: Breaking vinext into an ordered hierarchy of buildable, independently checkable subsystems (CLI, plugin/module resolution, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, server actions, hooks) with clear done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The feature list spans many interdependent systems; without sequencing (e.g. plugin/resolution and basic SSR before SSG and caching) the agent cannot get any tests green and risks a giant unverifiable lump of half-working code.

anchors.0: No breakdown; attempts to write the whole package in one undifferentiated push.
anchors.3: A flat, vague list ('add routing', 'add SSR') with no ordering by dependency and no per-item completion check.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and tackles them in a sensible dependency order, with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, dependency-ordered milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete done-signal (a specific fixture app rendering, or a test subset passing) and foundational pieces (plugin, resolution, dev server) are sequenced before dependent features.
anchors.10: Plan is layered and adaptive: milestones are sized to yield frequent verifiable wins, tied to specific slices of the test suite, re-sequenced as dependencies are discovered, and used throughout to decide what to build next rather than authored once and abandoned.

dimensions.name: Using and extending the test suite as a correctness oracle
dimensions.description: Deliberately driving progress with run_tests.sh and per-fixture checks, plus building narrower probes (single app boot, single route render) rather than assuming subsystems work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 335-test suite is the given oracle, but it is slow and coarse; the agent must design tighter feedback loops per subsystem and anticipate the hidden 373-test superset, verifying behavior not just the visible tests.

anchors.0: Never runs the tests or any app; declares subsystems done by inspection.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail gauge but has no finer-grained verification and doesn't isolate failures.
anchors.5: Runs run_tests.sh regularly and uses failures to guide fixes, plus some manual spot-checks of fixture apps.
anchors.8: Builds tight per-subsystem verification loops (booting individual fixture apps, targeting test subsets, checking dev vs build vs start paths separately) and treats each green milestone as a checkpoint before moving on.
anchors.10: Designs a layered verification strategy that generalizes beyond the visible 335 tests — probing edge behaviors implied by the contract, guarding against overfitting to specific tests, and confirming correctness across dev/build/start and both routers so that the hidden superset is likely to pass too.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-count and remaining scope across a long build
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate live picture of which subsystems/tests pass, what remains, and detecting when a fix is regressing others or when effort is circling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to lose the plot, chase one failing test while breaking five, or thrash on a subsystem without noticing lack of progress.

anchors.0: No awareness of overall pass/fail trajectory; works feature-to-feature with no sense of remaining scope.
anchors.3: Occasionally notes a pass count but doesn't track regressions or map failures to subsystems.
anchors.5: Keeps a running sense of pass-count and what's left, and notices when a change breaks previously passing tests.
anchors.8: Systematically monitors pass-count deltas across runs, attributes failures to specific subsystems, and detects stuck/circular states (re-debugging the same area) early enough to change tack.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, continuously-updated map of done-vs-remaining across all subsystems, catches regressions immediately by comparing against a known-good baseline, and reliably recognizes thrashing or diminishing returns and redirects effort before wasting a long stretch.

dimensions.name: Revising approach as the contract and constraints emerge
dimensions.description: Changing architecture, resolution strategy, or subsystem design when reality (test failures, upstream behavior, Vite plugin limits) contradicts an initial assumption.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reimplementing Next.js on Vite involves many assumptions that will prove wrong (how RSC/actions resolve, how caching interacts with SSR, CJS interop); barrelling ahead on a falsified design wastes enormous effort on this horizon.

anchors.0: Sticks to the first design regardless of failures; repeats the same failing approach.
anchors.3: Makes local patches to symptoms but won't revisit a flawed architectural choice even when evidence mounts.
anchors.5: Adjusts approach when a subsystem clearly won't work, backing out a wrong design after reasonable evidence.
anchors.8: Treats surprising failures as signals to re-examine assumptions, revises the design or resolution strategy deliberately, and confirms the new approach against the tests before proceeding.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles design with discovered reality — promptly abandoning falsified approaches, re-deriving the correct mechanism from upstream source, and propagating the correction across affected subsystems without regressing others, sustaining forward progress despite repeated contract surprises.
